plot_extraction.response_text:
Stranded alone at college on Christmas Eve after illness cancels a planned holiday visit with his roommate’s family, wealthy student Satherwaite sinks into self-pity. While tidying his room, he finds a notebook borrowed from Doyle, a hardworking student outside his affluent social circle, and decides to return it.

Satherwaite discovers Doyle hosting a modest Christmas party for six students unable to go home. Though his arrival initially makes everyone uncomfortable, he chooses to stay and gradually wins the group over with humor, humility, and his willingness to join their simple festivities. The men share memories, light a tiny tree, exchange inexpensive comic gifts, and ask Satherwaite to play Santa Claus. Touched when they improvise a gift for him—a cheap red memorandum book—he secretly adds a paper knife he has just bought and presents it to Doyle.

The evening ends with songs and Christmas greetings at midnight. Satherwaite leaves wearing their cranberry garland and carrying a borrowed old pipe, now accepted as a friend. A playful snowball exchange follows, and he walks away no longer lonely, having found genuine warmth and fellowship in an unexpected place.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is written in a polished early-twentieth-century collegiate realism, combining social comedy, Christmas sentiment, and a gentle moral arc. Its setting is rendered through recognisable period details—telegram forms, boarding houses, college clubs, proctors, smoking pipes, waistcoats, streetcars, and class-year designations such as “‘02”—which give the narrative a distinctly upper-class New England university atmosphere. The story initially contrasts Satherwaite’s affluent, mahogany-and-cut-glass surroundings with Doyle’s shabby but homelike room, using physical space to dramatise the difference between material comfort and genuine fellowship.

The narration is third-person and closely aligned with Satherwaite’s consciousness. Although the narrator sometimes supplies background information or makes general observations, most scenes are filtered through the protagonist’s moods, assumptions, and self-conscious calculations. This produces a mild form of free indirect discourse: phrases such as “Phil would keep; and so would Phil’s sister” or “By Jove, he would stay” carry Satherwaite’s own idiom into the narrative voice. The narrator treats him with affectionate irony, exposing his vanity, privilege, and theatrical self-pity without making him unsympathetic. His conviction that he is the most miserable person in New England, his careful selection of a waistcoat to impress Phil’s sister, and his notion that tidying a room might consume an evening all establish him as spoiled but fundamentally good-hearted.

The prose is expansive, fluent, and conventionally literary. Sentences are often long and cumulative, especially when describing movement, surroundings, or a sequence of thoughts. The opening sentence strings together a succession of physical actions before arriving at Satherwaite staring into the fire, immediately conveying restless irritation. Semicolons, em dashes, parenthetical qualifications, and balanced clauses are frequent. Short sentences and fragments—“Satherwaite was troubled,” “And now--!” or “Satherwaite was thinking”—punctuate these longer constructions, giving emphasis to changes of mood. The syntax is controlled rather than experimental, and its formal narrative poise contrasts pleasantly with the loose, colloquial speech of the students.

The diction mixes genteel literary vocabulary with period slang. Descriptive language includes words such as “untenanted,” “perfunctorily,” “assemblage,” “melancholia,” and “benignant,” while the dialogue is full of expressions like “awfully,” “jolly,” “old man,” “beggar,” “By Jove,” “Great Scott,” “baccy,” and “chop it off.” This contrast helps define the social milieu and gives the conversations a buoyant, youthful quality. Class difference is registered less through dialect than through possessions, habits, furnishings, and social confidence. Doyle and his friends speak standard English, but their worn clothes, cheap gifts, battered furniture, and financial limitations distinguish them from Satherwaite’s circle.

Dialogue is central to the story’s tonal and emotional development. At first it is stiff, hesitant, and crowded with polite evasions, reflecting the group’s suspicion of Satherwaite and his awareness that he is intruding. Repetitions, interruptions, false starts, and qualifying phrases reproduce embarrassment: Doyle’s “little—a sort of a Christmas-eve party” is characteristic. As mutual trust grows, the dialogue becomes quicker, louder, and more playful, with teasing, exclamations, mock ceremoniousness, and collective responses. The recurring phrase “Chop it off!” becomes a sign that Satherwaite has entered the group’s informal social language. Speech therefore does more than provide liveliness; it measures his transition from outsider to companion.

Characterisation is largely behavioural and relational. Satherwaite’s development appears through small acts: accepting Doak’s battered pipe without condescension, entertaining the gathering with a self-mocking account of his misfortune, valuing the cheap memorandum book, and discreetly placing his paper knife among the gifts. These gestures soften the class barrier without requiring an explicit declaration of reform. The other students are sketched rapidly through memorable physical or biographical details—the faded cricket blazer, eaglelike face, heavy whiskers, scholarships, debates, and homes far away. They remain a collective “gang” more than fully individualised figures, which suits their function as an embodiment of fellowship.

The tone moves from comic petulance through social discomfort to warmth and restrained sentiment. Early humour is directed at Satherwaite’s disproportionate misery and privileged expectations. In Doyle’s room, the comedy becomes more communal, arising from awkwardness, inexpensive joke gifts, student banter, and improvised ritual. The sentimental passages are carefully prepared by concrete sensory imagery: tobacco haze, firelight, tiny candles, cranberries, popcorn, snow, frosted streetcar windows, and mellow light. The story’s most lyrical moment pauses over the silent blue-white city outside the window, briefly suspending the joking atmosphere and allowing Christmas feeling to emerge without overt preaching.

The pacing is linear and scene-driven. A relatively brisk opening establishes the failed holiday plan, after which retrospective summary explains Satherwaite’s afternoon and his social background. The walk to Doyle’s room acts as a transition, while the visit itself unfolds in increasingly detailed real time. The initial awkwardness is deliberately prolonged through silences, glances, and the business of finding a chair and pipe. Once Satherwaite wins acceptance, the pace accelerates through anecdotes, gift-giving, singing, and midnight greetings. The ending extends the newfound intimacy into physical action: the snowball exchange transforms the winter street from a symbol of loneliness into a space of play.

Imagery is strongly organised around contrasts. Darkness is opposed to firelight and candlelight; cold streets to warm interiors; wealth to shabbiness; isolation to fellowship; expensive abundance to emotionally meaningful trifles. Satherwaite’s grand room is initially lifeless, whereas Doyle’s cramped study is animated by flames, smoke, conversation, and homemade decorations. Gifts carry particular symbolic force. Satherwaite’s costly paper knife seems “useless” beside the cheap comic presents, yet it becomes meaningful through spontaneous generosity; conversely, the inexpensive red memorandum book matters to him because it signifies acceptance. Material value is thus displaced by emotional and communal value.

The story’s structure follows a compact conversion pattern. Satherwaite begins absorbed in disappointment, romantic expectation, and social rank. His accidental visit exposes him to people he has casually regarded as belonging to another “coterie.” He initially stays partly from loneliness and partly from pride, wanting to disprove their assumption that he is a snob. Nevertheless, performance gradually becomes sincerity: his tact and charm open the group to him, while their modest celebration awakens in him a new appreciation of family, tradition, and uncomplicated companionship. The transformation is understated and credible because his essential personality does not change; his sociability and generosity simply find a less self-centred direction.

Overall, the style is genial, ironic, observant, and ultimately affirmative. It belongs to the tradition of periodical holiday fiction in which a temporary crisis produces moral recognition and social reconciliation. Its sentiment is tempered by humour, its moral is embodied in objects and interactions rather than stated directly, and its closing note is energetic rather than solemn. The final laughter and snowballs leave the reader with an image of spontaneous fellowship, completing the movement from a solitary man brooding before an elegant fireplace to a young man joyfully hailed by new friends in the snow.

## The Red Memorandum Book

Satherwaite opened the lower drawer of his bureau, shut it with unnecessary violence, crossed the room, rearranged three silver-backed brushes which were already in an irreproachable line, glanced at the clock, and then dropped into the great leather chair before the fire, where he sat with his chin in his hand and regarded the coals as though they, too, had failed him at the last moment.

It was five o’clock on Christmas Eve, and he was, he had decided, the most miserable man in New England.

At four he had received Phil Cushing’s telegram:

FATHER DOWN WITH GRIP DOCTOR FORBIDS GUESTS AWFULLY SORRY LETTER FOLLOWS MERRY CHRISTMAS PHIL

The message lay on the rug where Satherwaite had allowed it to fall. Its yellow envelope, propped against the brass fender, wore an air of official finality. The whole beautiful scheme of the holiday had collapsed in nineteen words, of which “Merry Christmas” seemed to him the most wantonly offensive.

For ten days he had been looking forward to the visit. There would have been the journey north in the smoking compartment with Phil; the great square Cushing house, full of cousins and holly and old servants; skating, perhaps, on the river; a dance at the Assembly Rooms; and, above all, Phil’s sister Margaret, whom Satherwaite had met only twice and had remembered with remarkable persistence. For Margaret’s possible approval he had purchased a dark green waistcoat of a distinction so discreet that it had cost almost twice as much as a more assertive garment. It lay now upon the bed, between two tissue papers, useless and reproachful.

Phil would keep; and so, presumably, would Phil’s sister. But Christmas would not.

Most of the college had gone down on the noon trains. His own family were in California, where his mother had declared they were having a “quite absurd Christmas among roses,” and the club dining room was closed until Thursday. He might have taken a train for New York and spent the day with an aunt, but the aunt had three small children and a husband who collected ecclesiastical snuffboxes. Besides, the useful trains had gone. The last car for Boston would place him in a hotel at an hour when hotels became intolerably conscious of being hotels.

He poked the fire. His room was one of the pleasantest in the Yard: mahogany shelves, deep crimson curtains, two old sporting prints, cut-glass decanters upon a tray, and a mantelpiece broad enough to accommodate photographs of the persons whom, at various times, Satherwaite had thought it proper to admire. Yet the room had never appeared so large or so completely untenanted. Even the fire burned with a decorous reserve, as though engaged for the evening elsewhere.

“What the deuce does a man do on Christmas Eve?” he demanded aloud.

The room offered no suggestion.

He considered reading. There was a new novel on the table, but the hero was a young duke whose matrimonial embarrassments seemed, under present circumstances, trivial. He considered writing letters and rejected the proposal as morbid. Finally, with the desperate courage of one who faces an unexampled calamity, he resolved to put his room in order.

For twenty minutes he laboured. He burned old invitations, placed seven collars in a drawer, restored a racquet to its press, and gathered into a pile the notebooks, pamphlets, and stray papers that had accumulated under the window seat. The occupation did not consume the evening, as he had rather hoped it might. It did, however, disclose a black composition book with “M. F. Doyle, ’02” written across the cover.

Satherwaite held it up and frowned.

Then he remembered. Doyle had lent him the notebook after Bevan’s lecture on constitutional history, when Satherwaite had been absent at the Yale game and had discovered, somewhat late, that Bevan’s lectures might be represented upon the examination. Doyle had copied them in a small, painstaking hand, with dates underlined and references entered in the margin. Satherwaite had thanked him, meant to return the book, and forgotten it.

He knew Doyle slightly. Everybody knew him slightly. Doyle sat in the first row, wore shiny coats, won scholarships, and spoke at debates in a dry, deliberate fashion which made careless men uncomfortable. He belonged to no club of consequence; indeed, it had never occurred to Satherwaite that Doyle belonged anywhere. Yet he recalled that the fellow lived in a boarding house beyond the Square, over a stationer’s shop.

The notebook supplied an errand, and an errand, at five-thirty on Christmas Eve, had the dignity of a destination. Satherwaite wrapped himself in his ulster, thrust the book into his pocket, and went out.

The Yard was blue with the early dusk. Snow had begun falling—not vigorously, but in fine, speculative flakes that hovered about the lamps and silvered the bare elms. The windows of the dormitories were chiefly dark. Here and there a proctor’s light shone with official persistence, and from one distant entry came the melancholy sound of a piano played by somebody who knew only the first half of “The Palms.”

Outside the gates the little shops were closing. Boys hurried past with parcels; a streetcar, its windows clouded with frost, clanged toward Boston; and a stout gentleman carrying a turkey nearly collided with Satherwaite at the crossing. All the world seemed provided with a household, a parcel, or at least a turkey. Satherwaite had only Doyle’s notebook.

The stationer’s shop was dark, but a side door admitted him to a narrow hallway smelling of boiled cabbage and damp wool. On the second floor a baby was crying; on the third, some one laughed, and a chair scraped over bare boards. Satherwaite found Doyle’s name on a visiting card tacked beside a door at the top.

He knocked.

There was an abrupt silence within—not the silence of an empty room, but the much more expressive silence of several persons who have stopped talking at once. Then came a movement, a whisper, and Doyle opened the door.

For an instant he merely stared.

“Satherwaite!”

“Hallo, Doyle. I found your notebook and thought I’d bring it round.”

“Oh!” Doyle took the book, looked at it, and looked again at Satherwaite. “That was very good of you. I shouldn’t have wanted you to trouble—especially to-night.”

“No trouble at all.”

Behind Doyle, Satherwaite saw a small room crowded with men. One sat on a trunk, one on the arm of a horsehair sofa, and two were kneeling beside a tiny evergreen set in a soap box. There were cranberries on a string, a bowl of popcorn, pipes, newspapers, and six faces turned toward the doorway with varying expressions of curiosity and dismay.

Doyle became aware of the pause.

“We’re having a little—a sort of Christmas-eve party,” he explained. “Some of the fellows who couldn’t get home. It isn’t much of an affair.”

“It looks jolly,” said Satherwaite.

The remark, though kindly intended, was received with caution. A tall man in a faded cricket blazer stopped chewing a cranberry. Somebody behind him hastily removed a paper cap from his head.

Doyle cleared his throat. “Won’t you come in for a minute?”

The invitation was polite; it was also, Satherwaite perceived, constructed in the expectation that he would refuse. He might have done so. He was overdressed for the room, socially unexplained, and suddenly conscious of his gloves, his stick, and the faint odour of good cigars that clung to his ulster. These men knew him as one of the fellows who dined behind club windows, drove hired tandems, and forgot borrowed notebooks. His departure would relieve them all.

Then from below there floated upward the sound of the baby, still crying with patient despair; beyond the hall window snow pressed softly against the dark; and Satherwaite remembered his own splendid fire burning alone.

“Thanks,” he said. “I’d like to, if you mean it.”

Doyle’s eyebrows rose. “Of course I mean it. Come in.”

Introductions followed. The man in the blazer was Crandall, ’01, who had once made forty-three runs against Princeton and would probably retain the blazer until it fell from him by natural dissolution. The broad, bewhiskered senior by the fireplace was Doak of Minnesota; he had missed his train through work at the laboratory. Pell was the small, eagle-faced debater; Ashmore, the long youth on the trunk, came from Oregon and could not afford the journey; Rugg had intended to go home to Vermont, but his younger brothers had scarlet fever; and the round-faced freshman called Beale had discovered that a money order expected from an uncle did not exist.

“My uncle is a man of imagination,” Beale explained. “He imagines he sent it.”

There was a slight laugh, after which constraint returned.

Doyle took Satherwaite’s coat and encountered difficulty in finding a place for it. At last he hung it over the corner of a bookcase, where its sable collar appeared indecently sumptuous. Satherwaite was offered the only sound chair. He declined it and sat on an upturned packing case, thereby producing a second, more approving silence.

“Smoke?” said Doak.

“Thanks.”

Doak extended a leather pouch whose condition suggested service in several campaigns.

“It’s not club tobacco,” he said. “It may kill you.”

“If it does, don’t send word to my family until after Christmas.”

Doak’s whiskers moved. “Take my pipe too. The stem pulls out, but you can hold it in with your thumb.”

The pipe was old, black, and formidable. Satherwaite accepted it without examination, filled it, and applied a match. At the second inhalation his eyes watered, but he continued heroically.

“Good baccy,” he said, when speech became possible.

“Liar,” observed Crandall.

It was the first word addressed to him without ceremony, and Satherwaite felt absurdly pleased.

The room itself, now that he had leisure to observe it, was shabby to the point of ingenuity. A green curtain concealed a washstand; the carpet had been cut and reassembled from at least two former carpets; the mantel clock lacked a minute hand, and the gas fixture leaned from the wall as if wearied by education. Yet the fire snapped generously in a little iron grate. Books stood everywhere in tight, industrious ranks. Over the windows hung branches of hemlock, and on the table was a supper of sandwiches, apples, doughnuts, cheese, and a brown jug whose contents Doyle guarded with some vigilance from Beale.

The tiny tree occupied the centre. It was scarcely three feet high and leaned eastward, but the men had adorned it with cranberries, popcorn, gilt stars cut from tobacco boxes, and little parcels tied in red string. A white clay pipe served as an angel.

“That’s a good-looking tree,” said Satherwaite.

“It has character,” Pell replied. “The man who sold it called it damaged.”

“Chop it off!” said Crandall.

This phrase was evidently established among them. Whenever a statement became too grand, too personal, or too nearly sentimental, somebody cried, “Chop it off!” and the offender was expected to subside. Satherwaite stored the custom away for future use.

For a time the conversation moved painfully. They discussed the weather, the emptiness of the Yard, the probability that Hollis would be elected captain, and the injustice of Professor Bevan’s marking. Each topic expired after a few exchanges. Satherwaite could feel the party waiting for him to go, and pride, loneliness, and a genuine desire not to spoil their evening combined to make him determined to stay until they wanted him.

Doyle attempted rescue.

“You were to have gone away, weren’t you?”

“Yes. Phil Cushing asked me up to his place.”

“And you changed your mind?”

“My mind had very little to do with it. His father developed the grip at a strategically perfect hour.”

“That’s hard luck,” said Rugg.

“It was worse than that. It was tragedy. You fellows don’t know what preparations had been made.” Satherwaite leaned forward, warming to his theme. “For ten days I’ve been engaged in becoming the sort of person a respectable family might permit in its house. I bought a waistcoat.”

“Great Scott!” said Doak.

“A green one—very quiet, very distinguished. The shopman assured me it expressed character without ostentation. I had my hair cut. I answered a note from my aunt. I even attended chapel twice.”

“Twice?” Beale breathed.

“On consecutive mornings. And then, at four to-day, I receive nineteen brutal words from Cushing, including a Merry Christmas which I regard as actionable.”

They laughed—not politely this time, but with the quick recognition of men who perceive that another is willing to make game of himself. Satherwaite drew Phil’s telegram from his pocket and read it with the solemnity of a death announcement.

“Father down with grip,” Pell repeated. “Do you suspect foul play?”

“I suspect Margaret.”

“Who’s Margaret?” asked Crandall.

Satherwaite hesitated just long enough.

“Phil’s sister.”

A roar greeted this. Doak slapped his knee; Beale fell against the tree and was dragged away by Doyle; even the austere Pell grinned.

“A waistcoat!” cried Crandall. “He bought it for a girl!”

“I bought it for myself,” said Satherwaite with dignity. “The girl was merely to be permitted to see it.”

“Chop it off!” they shouted together.

After that the party became possible.

The brown jug contained cider, heated with cloves and a quantity of sugar which Beale had measured under the theory that no beverage could be injured by sweetness. Doyle filled mugs, apologized for their differing sizes, and was told by everybody to chop it off. Sandwiches went round. Satherwaite ate three and declared the potted meat superior to anything at his club.

“No club talk,” warned Ashmore.

“Quite right. Vulgar subject.”

“Especially to those who don’t belong,” Pell said dryly.

The remark produced a little eddy of discomfort. Doyle glanced at him; Crandall frowned. Satherwaite, who might yesterday have taken offence, examined his broken pipe.

“You have the advantage of me there,” he said. “Some of us don’t belong nearly so much as we think we do.”

Pell looked up sharply. Then he nodded.

“Fair enough.”

The moment passed, and something passed with it. Satherwaite ceased to be a visitor whom they must entertain. Doak asked whether he played whist; Crandall demanded his opinion of the football coaches; Beale borrowed his matches without permission. When the minute-less clock had, according to Doyle’s watch, reached eight, each man was obliged to tell of the best Christmas he remembered.

Rugg described a Vermont farmhouse snowed to the second-storey windows, with twenty cousins sleeping in feather beds and his grandfather carving a turkey of mythological proportions. Ashmore spoke of an Oregon logging camp where his father had once brought home a sack of oranges after three days on horseback. Doak remembered sleigh bells across a Minnesota lake. Crandall’s story concerned a cricket bat, though nobody understood why a cricket bat had been required in December. Beale confessed that his best Christmas had been at twelve, when an elderly neighbour, believing him to be a poor orphan, gave him two dinners.

“I had parents,” Beale explained, “but it seemed discourteous to mention them.”

When Satherwaite’s turn came, he thought first of a Christmas at Newport, with footmen, silver candelabra, and a cotillion at which every favour had come from Paris. Yet what he told them was something he had nearly forgotten: an afternoon when he was seven, walking home through snow with his father, each carrying one end of a wooden sled. His father had died two years later.

“No reason it should have been the best,” Satherwaite concluded, looking into the fire. “Nothing happened.”

Nobody spoke for a moment.

Then Crandall said gently, “Chop it off.”

They all laughed, Satherwaite loudest.

At nine they lighted the tree. The operation required courage. The candles had been cut in half and fastened to the branches with wire; one leaned against a cranberry and another immediately set fire to a gilt star. Doak extinguished it between his fingers. The gas was turned low, and the poor little evergreen stood luminous in the dim room, its popcorn casting gigantic shadows upon the wall, its clay angel tipped drunkenly toward the ceiling.

Outside, the snow had thickened. It descended beyond the panes in a blue-white hush, hiding chimneys, softening roofs, and making the narrow street seem remote from every troubled and calculating part of the world. A streetcar passed at the farther corner, glowing through the storm like a travelling room; then its bell diminished, and the city was still.

Satherwaite looked from the window to the six faces about the tree. The candlelight touched Crandall’s faded blazer, Doyle’s worn cuffs, the scar on Doak’s thumb, and the anxious care with which Beale shielded one flame from a draught. There was nothing handsome in the assemblage, nothing correctly appointed; yet the room possessed what his own had lacked. It was inhabited—not merely by bodies and voices, but by memories, kindnesses, the cheerful acceptance of disappointment, and that mysterious enlargement of space which occurs when no one is guarding his share of it.

Doyle turned up the gas.

“Presents!” cried Beale.

The parcels were distributed by a lottery of Doyle’s invention. No gift had cost more than twenty-five cents, and most were designed to insult the recipient. Pell, whose speeches habitually exceeded his allotted time, received an alarm clock without works. Crandall was given a pamphlet entitled The Care of Ancient Fabrics, in reference to his blazer. Doak got a diminutive comb for his whiskers; Ashmore, who was six feet four, a child’s tin sword; Rugg, a pair of paper cuffs; Doyle, a rubber stamp bearing the word REJECTED, with which to mark his poems; and Beale a toy bank containing a nickel firmly glued to the bottom.

The laughter became violent. The alarm clock was made to preside over the mantel; Crandall read aloud from The Care of Ancient Fabrics; Doak combed one whisker into a point and addressed Satherwaite in the manner of a German professor.

Then Doyle saw him watching and stopped.

“We’ve made a blunder,” he said.

“What’s that?”

“We’ve no present for you.”

“My dear fellow, I came without warning.”

“That doesn’t matter,” said Rugg. “Everybody gets a present.”

“Certainly,” Doak agreed. “It’s the Constitution.”

“Unwritten,” Pell added, “but binding.”

They conferred in a corner with much whispering and furtive inspection of pockets. Satherwaite protested, but was shouted down. Presently Beale ran into the hall and returned with a parcel wrapped in a page from the Boston Transcript. It was tied with the cranberry string that had earlier decorated the mantel.

Doyle cleared his throat.

“Satherwaite, the committee has learned with pain that you were decoyed into this gathering under false pretences and have remained in spite of the food. It therefore begs you to accept this slight token of—of—”

“Chop it off!” said Satherwaite.

“Of its esteem,” Doyle finished obstinately.

Inside the newspaper was a small red memorandum book, such as the stationer downstairs sold for ten cents. A label had been pasted across the cover, and upon it each man had signed his name. Underneath, Beale had written:

FOR ENGAGEMENTS NOT CANCELLED BY GRIP

The thing was absurd, cheap, and hastily contrived. Satherwaite held it for several seconds without opening it. He possessed a Russian leather engagement book with gilt edges, sent each year by his father’s bankers, and had never thought twice about it. This red book, bending already at one corner, seemed for the moment a possession of incomparable value.

“It’s ripping,” he said. “Thank you.”

His voice betrayed him slightly. Crandall began, “Chop—” but stopped.

Satherwaite slipped the book into his inner pocket. His fingers touched a narrow parcel there, and he remembered the paper knife.

He had bought it that afternoon for Phil—a small silver paper knife with Phil’s initials on the handle—and had intended to take it north. It was not an extravagant gift by Satherwaite’s standards, but among the alarm clock and rubber stamp it would look barbarously expensive. To present it openly would be to disturb the delicate equality of their nonsense. Yet he wished suddenly and urgently to give something.

While Beale was attempting to open the toy bank with Ashmore’s tin sword, Satherwaite moved behind the tree. One little package remained beneath it: Doyle’s rubber stamp had been wrapped in two parts, and the empty lower paper still lay there. He took out the paper knife, stripped away the jeweller’s covering, and folded it into the discarded paper. The initials—P.C.—were an embarrassment. After an instant’s thought he drew his pencil and added, in small letters upon a scrap:

For cutting the pages of books you have time to read because other men borrow your notes.

He tucked the parcel under a branch.

“Hallo,” he said. “There’s another one.”

Doyle looked surprised. “For whom?”

“It says Doyle.”

“But I’ve had mine.”

“Constitution allows two,” said Satherwaite. “Unwritten, but binding.”

Doyle opened the parcel. The room quieted when the silver flashed.

“This isn’t one of ours,” he said.

“Apparently Santa Claus has better taste than the rest of you.”

Doyle read the slip, glanced toward Satherwaite, and understood. For a moment he seemed about to object. Then, perhaps perceiving that objection would injure more than acceptance, he ran his thumb along the blade.

“I’ve never had one,” he said simply. “Thank you—Santa Claus.”

“Satherwaite ought to be Santa Claus!” Beale exclaimed.

The suggestion was instantly adopted. A red table cover was taken from the stand, a cushion was tied about Satherwaite’s middle, and cotton from the soap box was arranged under his chin. Crandall contributed the cranberry garland as a chain of office. Thus attired, Satherwaite sat in Doyle’s chair and delivered judgments upon the company.

To Pell he granted concision; to Doak, a pipe whose stem remained in place; to Ashmore, another inch of height “to remove all remaining inconvenience from ceilings”; to Rugg, immunity from scarlet fever; to Crandall, a new blazer, which Crandall rejected as an insult; to Beale, an uncle of unimpeachable financial memory; and to Doyle—

Satherwaite paused.

“To Doyle,” he said, “the return of all borrowed property within a reasonable time.”

“Hear, hear!” cried Pell.

“And what do you grant yourself?” Doyle asked.

The laughter dwindled. Satherwaite looked around the shabby room, at the little tree, the steaming mugs, and the men who three hours earlier had wished him politely out of the doorway.

“Another invitation,” he said.

This time no one cried, “Chop it off.”

“You’ve got it,” said Doak.

They sang after that. None had a beautiful voice, and several had voices of unusual ugliness, but deficiencies of tune were corrected by vigour. They began with college songs, passed through “The Spanish Cavalier,” “Nellie Was a Lady,” and a ballad concerning a man who had loved six sisters in Ohio, and arrived at last, by common instinct, at the carols.

The fire sank lower; the candles guttered; tobacco smoke made a blue canopy beneath the ceiling. Satherwaite, with the red table cover about his shoulders and Doak’s pipe between his teeth, sang until his throat hurt. He had attended Christmas services in churches where paid choirs produced harmonies of angelic precision, but no music had ever seemed so honest as these seven untrained voices stumbling together through “God Rest Ye Merry, Gentlemen.”

At a quarter before twelve they carried their mugs to the window. The storm had ceased. Snow lay smooth along the roofs and window ledges; stars showed above the chimneys; and every ordinary object—the ash barrels, telegraph wires, shop awnings, and rails of the streetcar track—had acquired a temporary purity. Far off, bells began to sound.

“Not midnight yet,” said Doyle, consulting his watch.

“Your clock says it’s half past four,” Beale observed.

“My clock has always taken a broad view.”

They waited, suddenly subdued. Somewhere below, the baby had stopped crying. From a neighbouring house came a woman’s laugh and the thin notes of a parlour organ. Satherwaite thought of his mother among California roses; of Phil at the Cushing place, creeping past his father’s sickroom; of Margaret, perhaps fastening holly to a stair rail; and of his own vacant chamber, where the green waistcoat lay in tissue paper before an unwatched fire.

He did not pity himself.

Doyle lifted his hand.

“Now.”

“Merry Christmas!” they shouted.

Hands met across the table. Crandall pounded Satherwaite on the shoulder; Beale embraced Doak and became entangled in the whiskers; Pell, who disapproved of emotional display, shook everybody’s hand twice. Doyle came last.

“Merry Christmas, Satherwaite.”

“Merry Christmas, old man.”

There was no more to say, which was fortunate.

It was nearly one when Satherwaite put on his ulster. The cranberry chain remained around his neck because Beale insisted it was an honorary decoration. Doak’s pipe remained in his pocket because Doak insisted it should be smoked on the way home.

“But it’s your pipe.”

“I have another.”

“You said this was the only one seasoned properly.”

“I lied. Take it, you beggar.”

Doyle walked with him to the lower door. The narrow hall had grown colder, and the gas jet burned very low.

“I’m glad you came,” Doyle said.

“So am I.”

“I thought at first—well, we all thought you’d be bored.”

“I was at first,” Satherwaite replied gravely.

Doyle stared; then Satherwaite grinned.

“Chop it off,” said Doyle, and pushed him into the snow.

The street was white and empty. Satherwaite had gone six paces when something struck the back of his hat and scattered cold powder down his collar. He turned. Six figures occupied the upper windows, Beale foremost, armed with a washbasin full of snow gathered from the sill.

“Assassins!” Satherwaite cried.

He made a snowball and threw it. It burst against the bricks a yard below the window.

“Club training!” Pell called down.

“Rotten form!” shouted Crandall.

A second missile struck Satherwaite’s shoulder. He dropped his stick, made two snowballs with care, and returned the fire. One entered the open window and produced a yell from Doak; the other removed the clay pipe from the top of the tree.

“Run!” Doyle called. “The proctor’s coming!”

No proctor was visible, but Satherwaite seized his stick and ran, laughing, while snowballs broke behind him and the men at the windows shouted contradictory Christmas greetings. At the corner he turned, lifted his hat, and bowed with all the magnificence the cranberry garland allowed.

Then he went on alone.

Yet the street no longer appeared lonely. The snow creaked companionably beneath his boots; Doak’s deplorable pipe bulged in his pocket; the red memorandum book rested over his heart; and from the lighted room behind him came a final chorus, ragged, loud, and affectionate:

“Merry Christmas, Santa Claus!”

Satherwaite waved without looking back. A snowball, thrown with heroic but inaccurate zeal, sailed over his head and vanished into the immaculate night.

The town of Bellwether had no bells.

There had been bells once: bronze church bells, silver shop bells, brass handbells carried by the night watch. But long before Mara Venn was born, lightning struck the eastern tower and melted its great bell into a blackened lump. The smaller bells vanished soon afterward. Some were sold, some stolen, and some simply fell silent from rust.

Yet every morning at precisely six, the people of Bellwether woke to ringing.

No one knew where it came from.

The sound rolled over the slate roofs and narrow streets in three solemn notes. It trembled in window glass, rippled the river, and sent roosting birds into the pale sky. At noon, the bells rang six bright notes. At midnight, they rang once, so deep that sleepers felt it in their bones.

The townspeople had learned not to question it.

Mara had not.

She was seventeen and apprenticed to Harlan Venn, her grandfather, the town’s last clockmaker. His shop stood between a bakery and a boarded-up theater, its windows crowded with watches, cuckoo clocks, hourglasses, and mechanical birds. Nothing in the shop showed the correct time.

“Accuracy is easy,” Harlan often said. “Meaning is difficult.”

Mara suspected this was his excuse for never repairing the clock above the door, which had been stuck at thirteen minutes past four for as long as she could remember.

Each morning, when the invisible bells rang, Harlan stopped whatever he was doing. He bowed his head and counted the notes.

“There are always three,” Mara told him one rainy morning.

“So far,” he replied.

She looked up from the pocket watch she was dismantling. “Do you know where they come from?”

Harlan adjusted the lens clipped over his right eye. “Some questions are traps.”

“That sounds like something people say when they don’t know the answer.”

“Or when they know it too well.”

He selected a pair of tweezers and lifted a gear no bigger than a grain of rice. His hands were spotted with age, but they never shook while working.

Mara leaned closer. “Do they come from under the town?”

The gear slipped.

It fell onto the wooden table with a tiny, betraying click.

Harlan stared at it.

Then he removed his lens and said, “Why would you ask that?”

“Because I listened at the old well yesterday. At noon.”

The old well stood in Founder’s Square, dry and covered by an iron grate. Children were warned not to play near it, although no one could remember anyone ever falling in.

“When the bells rang,” Mara continued, “I heard them below me. Not above. The sound came up through the stones.”

Harlan’s face tightened. “Stay away from that well.”

“Why?”

“Because I said so.”

“You also say never to trust a clock with painted numbers.”

“That is excellent advice.”

“And equally unexplained.”

Harlan pushed back his chair. For a moment, Mara thought he would shout. Instead, he crossed the shop and turned the sign in the window from OPEN to CLOSED.

“Go upstairs,” he said.

“Grandfather—”

“Now.”

She obeyed, but only as far as the landing. From there, hidden behind the banister, she watched him lock the front door and draw the curtains. He stood in the darkened shop, surrounded by ticking clocks, his shoulders bowed beneath a weight she could not see.

Then he took a small iron key from a chain around his neck.

He unlocked the bottom drawer of his workbench and removed a wooden box.

Inside lay a bell.

It was no larger than a walnut, black with age, and missing its clapper.

Harlan held it in both hands as if it were a living thing.

That night, Mara dreamed of a tower buried upside down beneath Bellwether. Its roots pierced the sky while its spire descended into darkness. A bell swung at the bottom, ringing without being struck.

When she woke, midnight’s single note was fading.

A second sound followed it.

A knock came from downstairs.

Mara sat up. Rain whispered against the roof. She waited.

Three more knocks.

She pulled on her boots and crept down. Harlan was already in the shop, carrying a candle. He opened the door only a hand’s width.

A woman stood outside in a gray traveling cloak. Rain streamed from its hood.

“You’re late,” Harlan said.

“The river flooded the north road.”

“You shouldn’t have come at all.”

“You sent for me.”

Mara recognized the woman’s voice before she saw her face. Elian Rook had been the town archivist until five years earlier, when she left without explanation. As a child, Mara had spent winter afternoons in the archives while Elian showed her maps and taught her to read old handwriting.

Elian stepped inside. A pale scar crossed her cheek, and her dark hair was threaded with silver.

“You still have it?” she asked.

Harlan glanced toward the stairs. Mara drew back into shadow.

“Yes,” he said.

“Then we may still have time.”

“For what?”

“The morning bells have changed.”

Harlan shook his head. “Three notes. Same as always.”

“Not the notes. The interval between them. Yesterday, each pause was one heartbeat shorter.”

Silence spread through the shop, disturbed only by a hundred indifferent clocks.

Elian lowered her voice. “It’s waking.”

Mara’s boot creaked against the stair.

Both adults turned.

There was no point hiding.

She descended with as much dignity as she could manage. “What is waking?”

Harlan closed his eyes.

Elian studied Mara, then gave a tired smile. “You’ve grown.”

“People do.”

“So I’ve heard.”

Harlan set the candle on the counter. “She stays here.”

“No,” Mara said.

“Mara.”

“You kept a secret under my feet all my life. You don’t get to send me to bed now.”

Elian looked amused. Harlan did not.

But after a long moment, he took the iron key from his neck.

“Get your coat,” he said.

They crossed Bellwether under heavy rain. Water rushed along the gutters and shone beneath the gas lamps. The square was empty. Above it rose the ruined eastern tower, its upper stones split by the ancient lightning strike.

Harlan led them to the old well.

Elian knelt and cleared mud from the iron grate. Beneath the town crest, almost hidden by rust, was a keyhole.

Harlan inserted his key.

The grate opened without a sound.

A spiral staircase descended into darkness.

Mara looked at her grandfather. “How deep?”

“Deeper than the river,” he said. “Not as deep as regret.”

“Is everything a riddle to you?”

“Only the things I’m ashamed of.”

They went down.

The staircase seemed endless. Water dripped from the walls, and their lantern threw warped shadows across old masonry. At first, Mara heard the rain above. Then she heard the river moving somewhere beyond the stones. Finally, there was only the scrape of their boots and a faint vibration like the hum of a gigantic machine.

At the bottom stood a door of green bronze.

There were words carved across it:

WHAT IS GIVEN MAY BE KEPT.  
WHAT IS KEPT MUST BE COUNTED.  
WHAT IS COUNTED WILL END.

Elian pressed her palm against the metal.

The door opened.

Beyond it stretched an underground chamber larger than Founder’s Square. Great pillars vanished into darkness overhead. Gears rose from the floor like iron houses, their teeth turning with impossible slowness. Chains thick as tree trunks trembled under tension. At the center of the chamber hung a bell.

It was vast.

Its rim hovered just above the stone floor. Strange symbols covered its dark surface, shifting whenever Mara looked away. No rope hung from it, and there was no clapper inside.

Still, it hummed.

Mara felt the vibration behind her eyes.

“What is this place?” she whispered.

“The reason Bellwether exists,” Elian said.

Harlan approached the bell. “Three hundred and twelve years ago, the first settlers found it here. The town wasn’t built beside the river for trade. It was built around this chamber so the bell could be guarded.”

“Guarded from whom?”

“From everyone.”

Elian lifted the lantern toward the machinery. “The bell does not mark hours. It keeps them.”

Mara waited for more.

When none came, she said, “That explains nothing.”

Harlan’s expression was grave. “Every person in Bellwether gives the bell a small portion of time. A few seconds each day. The machinery gathers it, stores it, and uses it to maintain something like a boundary.”

“Between what?”

“Our world,” Elian said, “and a place where time does not pass in one direction.”

Mara stared at the bell. “That’s impossible.”

“Yes,” Elian replied. “That is why it needs a boundary.”

A metallic groan rolled through the chamber. One of the massive gears shuddered. Rust fell like red snow.

Harlan walked to a control stand near the bell. Its face held twelve empty sockets arranged in a circle. Eleven contained small black bells without clappers.

One socket was empty.

Harlan drew the wooden box from his coat and opened it.

“The piece from your drawer,” Mara said.

He nodded. “A regulator. There were twelve originally. Each governed part of the mechanism. This one was removed.”

“By whom?”

Harlan did not answer.

Elian did. “By me.”

Mara turned to her.

“Five years ago,” Elian said, “I discovered that the council had been feeding more time into the bell than the founders intended. Not seconds. Years. They took them from prisoners, from the ill, from people no one would defend. The council called it necessary maintenance.”

Harlan’s voice was bitter. “Elian removed the regulator to stop them.”

“I thought the machine would shut down,” she said. “Instead, it began drawing tiny amounts of time from everyone in town. Not enough to notice at first.”

Mara remembered Mrs. Vale at the bakery, whose hair had gone white in a single winter. She remembered children who seemed to outgrow their clothes overnight. She thought of her own mother, dead at thirty-two from a sickness that made her age faster than any doctor could explain.

She looked at Harlan.

He could not meet her eyes.

“My mother knew, didn’t she?”

“She discovered it,” he said. “She tried to repair the mechanism.”

“And it killed her?”

“No.” His voice broke. “I did.”

The chamber seemed to contract around them.

Harlan gripped the edge of the control stand.

“The machine demanded a keeper. Someone had to guide the excess time into the boundary while the regulator was missing. Your mother volunteered, but I refused. I took her place—or meant to. At the final moment, she locked me outside the chamber.”

Mara could hardly breathe.

“She gave the bell twenty years,” he continued. “It should have been enough to keep the boundary sealed until I found Elian and recovered the regulator. But Elian had fled, and I…” He looked suddenly ancient. “I was a coward. I told myself the machine was stable. I told myself there was time.”

The huge gear groaned again.

A crack appeared along one iron tooth.

Elian took the black bell from the box. “There may not be any now.”

She placed it into the empty socket.

Nothing happened.

Then every clock Mara had ever heard seemed to strike at once.

The sound hurled them to the floor. The enormous bell swung though no hand touched it. Its rim passed through the stone without breaking it, and the chamber filled with images.

Mara saw Bellwether’s streets under summer sun, then buried in snow, then drowned beneath the river. She saw houses built, burned, and built again in the same breath. People crossed the square as children and reached the other side old and stooped. Birds flew backward into eggs. Rain rose from puddles toward the clouds.

At the center of it all stood the eastern tower, whole and shining, its great bell ringing.

A voice entered Mara’s mind.

NOT ENOUGH.

The machinery stopped.

The sudden silence was worse than the noise.

Along the bronze door, darkness seeped through the edges. It moved like smoke underwater. Inside it, Mara glimpsed stars being born and extinguished, flowers blooming into seeds, faces aging backward into nothing.

Elian staggered to the control stand. “The stored time is gone.”

“How long before the boundary fails?” Harlan asked.

Elian examined the dials. “Minutes.”

Harlan began unfastening his coat.

Mara knew at once what he intended.

“No.”

He looked at her. His face had become peaceful.

“It requires a keeper,” he said.

“You said my mother gave twenty years.”

“I have fewer than that left. But perhaps the repair will make them sufficient.”

“You don’t know.”

“No.”

Elian’s hands moved over the mechanism. “Harlan, wait. There may be another way.”

“There isn’t.”

Mara caught his wrist. “You don’t get to hide the truth for years and then turn your death into an apology.”

His eyes filled with pain. “I am not asking forgiveness.”

“Good.”

The darkness around the door thickened. Somewhere beyond it, something scratched against the bronze.

Mara looked at the twelve black bells. She looked at the words she had seen on the door.

What is given may be kept. What is kept must be counted. What is counted will end.

“Accuracy is easy,” she murmured.

Harlan frowned. “What?”

“Meaning is difficult.”

She ran to the mechanism and examined the sockets. Fine lines linked each regulator to a central dial. The dial had no numbers, only names—thousands of them, engraved in spirals. Townspeople. Generations of them.

The machine had always counted time in lives.

That was the flaw.

“Mara,” Elian said, “what are you doing?”

“Clocks don’t make time. They divide it.”

She took a screwdriver from Harlan’s coat pocket and forced it beneath the dial.

He seized her shoulder. “If you break the counter—”

“It won’t know how much to take.”

“Exactly.”

“Then maybe we stop paying it.”

The scratching became a pounding. The door bowed inward.

Elian understood first. “The boundary doesn’t need years,” she said. “It needs sequence. A steady direction.”

Mara wrenched the dial free.

Beneath it, countless delicate hands spun around a single pin.

“If it cannot count individual lives,” Elian continued, “it may draw from something larger.”

“The town?” Harlan asked.

Mara shook her head.

She looked up at the enormous bell.

“Not the town. The clocks.”

Harlan stared at her. Then, slowly, he smiled.

“Every clock in Bellwether,” he said. “Every watch. Every measured second.”

“Can it work?” Mara asked.

“Meaning,” he replied, “is difficult.”

He took the screwdriver and drove it into the central pin.

The mechanism screamed.

Far above them, across Bellwether, clocks began to strike.

Mantel clocks chimed in empty rooms. Watches rang inside drawers. The frozen clock above Harlan’s shop lurched forward. The clock in the council hall spun wildly, shedding years of dust. Mechanical birds burst from little doors and sang until their springs snapped.

All that measured time poured downward.

The black bells in the control stand began to tremble.

The darkness withdrew from the bronze door.

The giant gears turned.

Once.

Twice.

Then steadily.

The enormous bell sounded three notes.

The first contained every farewell ever spoken in Bellwether.

The second held every promise.

The third was the sound of a child taking a first breath.

Then the chamber became still.

Elian sank against a pillar, laughing and crying at once. Harlan leaned heavily on Mara.

“Did we do it?” she asked.

“We changed it,” he said. “That is not always the same thing.”

They climbed the staircase as dawn approached.

When they emerged into Founder’s Square, the rain had stopped. People stood in doorways and streets, dressed in nightclothes and coats, holding silent clocks.

The town hall clock showed seven different hours on its four faces.

Mr. Vale’s pocket watch ran backward. The baker’s kitchen timer had sprouted a tiny mechanical wing. Every clock in Harlan’s shop displayed thirteen minutes past four.

None would move again.

“What happens now?” Mara asked.

Elian looked toward the paling sky. “Bellwether will have to live without counting every moment.”

At six, no bells rang.

People waited uneasily. Some covered their ears, as if silence were louder than sound. The sun climbed over the eastern hill without permission from any clock.

For the first time in more than three centuries, the morning belonged only to itself.

In the weeks that followed, Bellwether changed.

Trains became impossible to schedule, so the stationmaster rang a handbell whenever a train appeared in the distance. Shops opened when their owners arrived and closed when they grew tired. Bread was baked until it smelled ready. School lessons lasted until the children understood or the teacher lost patience. The council protested, passed regulations, revised them, and eventually discovered that no one knew when meetings were supposed to begin.

People still aged, but no faster than they ought to.

Harlan removed the broken clock above his shop. In its place, Mara hung a painted sign:

VENN & VENN  
REPAIRS OF THINGS THAT MATTER

They no longer repaired clocks. Instead, they mended music boxes, spectacles, toys, compasses, and once a wooden leg that squeaked mournfully in wet weather.

Elian returned to the archives. She wrote the true history of Bellwether in a book she refused to date.

Years later—or perhaps only a collection of winters and summers—Harlan died in his sleep. He had become very old, though no one could say exactly how old. Mara buried him on a hill where he could hear the river.

In his pocket, she placed the tiny black bell.

Afterward, she returned to the shop and sat alone among the silent clocks. Evening softened the windows. Dust floated through bars of amber light.

For a moment, grief made the whole world seem stopped.

Then someone knocked.

A little girl stood outside holding a broken mechanical bird.

“Can you fix it?” she asked.

Mara examined the bent wing and the rusted spring.

“I don’t know,” she said. “But I can try.”

She opened the door.

Far beneath the town, the great bell moved in darkness, fed not by stolen years but by uncounted moments: bread rising, rivers running, hands meeting, doors opening. It kept no record of who gave what. It demanded no names. It simply listened as life passed above and turned that passing into music no one could hear.

Except, sometimes, when the weather was clear and all the town had gone quiet, Mara would wake just before dawn.

She would feel a single note trembling through the stones.

Not a warning.

Not a summons.

Only the deep and wordless sound of the world continuing.
